commenti.body: Maybe it’s just my inner cynic talking, but lately I’ve  had such little patience for these types of films. They just seem more and more like an exercise in existential meditation, and I just don’t have the patience or curiosity that I once did.

Enjoyed it a lot. Petzold does Rohmer in a way that isn't particularly original nor inventive, but neither was that the case by the time Rohmer was on the seasonal films. I agree with it being clinical, but perhaps that elevates the simplistic moments of beauty that are scattered throughout. In particular, the reading of Heine's Der Asra impacted me a lot.

I think Petzold also pulls of the dynamic between the woman and the main character. His high strung behavior leaves him constantly on the outside, solely by an incorrect view of himself as such. This too, becomes the root of his suffering. Such a stance is not uncommon, neither in myself nor people I surround myself with, but it often difficult to identify it from our own perspective. What makes it powerful is thus refusing to align with the main character, letting us instead perceive him from a perspective closer to the woman's and the roommate's.

This premiered on Criterion Channel this week. 

I don't think I got all the intertextuality..? I was left pretty underwhelmed. I get that Leon as a writer is observant and feeling a lot on the inside and not showing it in his curmudgeonly exterior. I've only seen a bit of Rohmer (La Collectionneusse) so I don't have the background that is maybe required to fully get this movie.

If someone wants to explain why it's a superb masterpiece, I'd appreciate it.
